cultivar: Seed-grown bushes descended from Indian (Kangra and Assam-region) stock introduced around 1900, with later local selections
processing: Mostly orthodox black tea from small farms: withered, rolled, oxidised and fired in local factories, sorted into whole-leaf and broken grades; some CTC is also made. Traditional Iranian tea is dried without added scent, although bergamot-flavoured versions exist for the domestic market.
harvest_season: Three picks from late April to September; the spring pick (chay-e bahareh, April to May) is prized and sold separately, the summer pick is the bulk, and the autumn pick is plainer.
appearance_dry: Thin, dark, loosely twisted leaves of mixed size with some reddish stems, less tightly made than Ceylon, with a sweet, hay-like smell.
appearance_liquor: Bright reddish amber, clear, lighter than a Ceylon or Assam at the same strength.
taste_profile: Light, smooth and gently sweet with a hay-and-dried-fruit note, low tannin and a clean finish; it is milder than imported tea, which Iranians either prize or hold against it.

brewing.notes: Iranian method: make a concentrate in a small teapot kept warm on top of a samovar or kettle for 10–15 minutes, then dilute in the glass to a clear amber. Serve in a small glass (estekan) with a sugar cube or rock candy held in the mouth, never milk.

vintage_note: Sold all year by brand and grade, blended across the season and not dated; the spring pick is the exception, offered separately as chay-e bahareh at a premium from May onwards. Iranian shelves are also full of imported tea (mostly Ceylon and Indian, some of it smuggled) sold under local brands, so 'Iranian tea' on a pack does not always mean Lahijan-grown leaf. Use within the year.
description:
Iran drinks tea the way other countries drink water, and most of what it grows comes from the green hills behind Lahijan in Gilan, the wet, mild Caspian province. The industry dates from around 1900, when the Iranian diplomat Mohammad Mirza Kashef al-Saltaneh brought tea plants and know-how back from India and planted them in Lahijan; his tomb in the town is now a tea museum and he is remembered as the father of Iranian tea.

Tea here is a smallholder crop: thousands of family plots on the hillsides, hand-picked from late April and sold to local factories that make orthodox black tea. The spring pick is the proud one, sold on its own as chay-e bahareh; the summer flush is the bulk of the year. Processing is straightforward and the leaf tends to be loosely made, which gives a lighter, softer cup than the tightly rolled teas of Sri Lanka that Iran also imports in huge quantities.

In the glass, Lahijan tea is smooth and gently sweet, with hay and dried fruit, low tannin and a clean finish, a tea built for sipping all day rather than for impact. It is brewed as a concentrate in a small pot kept warm on a samovar, diluted in the glass to a clear amber, and drunk with a sugar cube held between the teeth or with rock candy, dates or sweets; milk is unheard of. Brewed too strong it goes flat rather than bitter, so dilute generously.

Buy it from an Iranian grocer under a Lahijan or Gilan label, and look for the word bahareh (spring) if you want the best; most everyday Iranian brands are blends, and many 'Iranian' teas are actually Ceylon leaf packed locally, which is not a scandal, just worth knowing. Domestic bergamot-scented tea is also popular and should be labelled as such.

It pairs with saffron rock candy and with the walnut-stuffed sweets of the Caspian coast; and a comparison with Rize tea from across the border in Turkey shows how differently two neighbours brew essentially similar leaf.
sources_note: No dedicated Iranian tea article found on English Wikipedia ('Iranian tea' missing; 'Tea in Iran' redirects to 'Iranian cuisine'); the 'Lahijan' city article is used as the umbrella. Kashef al-Saltaneh's introduction of tea around 1900 and the Indian origin of the stock are well-known history but dates are approximate. The scale of imported/smuggled tea is widely reported but unquantified here.
history:
Lahijan, in Gilan on the Caspian side of Iran, is the historic capital of the country's tea. The usual story credits a diplomat returning from India with bringing the first plants. Firmer ground comes in 1934, when the first modern-style factory opened.

The industry grew into roughly 107 factories and about 32,000 hectares of hillside gardens making orthodox black tea, with a reddish cup and a delicate flavour. The slopes invite comparison with Darjeeling.

It has since fallen on hard times. Imports and smuggled tea undercut local growers, some gardens are now used only for grazing, several mills stand derelict or run at half capacity, and factory owners have moved into real estate on what used to be tea land.
